You can create a lifecycle rule to optimize your objects' storage\\ncosts throughout their lifetime.\\n\\nYou can define the scope of the lifecycle rule to all objects in your bucket or to\\nobjects\\nwith a shared prefix, certain object tags, or a certain object size.\\n\\nYou can specify one or more predefined actions for Amazon S3 to perform. There are\\ntwo types of\\nactions: *transition* and *expiration*. Transition actions define when objects transition to a storage\\nclass for less-frequently accessed objects. Expiration actions define when objects\\nare\\nremoved. The effect of these actions depends on the versioning state of your bucket\\nand\\nobjects. Transitions and expirations are asynchronous operations. Your S3 costs, however,\\nare updated as though transitions and expirations were immediate.\\n\\nAmazon S3 has a list of supported lifecycle transitions between storage classes. For\\nmore\\ninformation about which storage classes you can transition objects to and the constraints\\nof\\nobject size, minimum days, and cost considerations, see Supported transitions and related constraints.\\n\\nWhen you create a new S3 Lifecycle rule Amazon S3 applies a default behavior to your\\nLifecycle configuration that prevents objects smaller than 128 KB from being transitioned.\\nYou can allow smaller objects to transition by adding an **Object size** filter that specifies a smaller size to each applicable rule. Additionally, you can\\nchange the default transition behavior so that objects smaller than 128 KB will transition\\nto S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive. To do this, use the\\noptional `x-amz-transition-object-size-minimum-default` header in a PutBucketLifecycleConfiguration request.\\n\\nThe effects of expiration actions are permanent. To prevent accidental deletion, we\\nrecommend that you take precautions, such as enabling S3 Versioning, S3 Object Lock, multi-factor authentication (MFA) delete, or S3 Replication.\\n\\nUnder **Review transition and expiration actions**, you can also review how the specified actions work on the lifecycle of\\ncurrent and noncurrent versions of objects.\\n\\nThere are per-request transition charges to move data into any supported S3 storage\\nclass\\nand charges to store the transitioned objects in the storage class. To do this, use the optional `x-amz-transition-object-size-minimum-default` header in a PutBucketLifecycleConfiguration request.\\n\\nThe effects of expiration actions are permanent. To prevent accidental deletion, we\\nrecommend that you take precautions, such as enabling\\nS3 Versioning, S3 Object Lock, multi-factor authentication (MFA) delete, or S3 Replication.\\n\\nUnder **Review transition and expiration actions**, you can also review how the specified actions work on the lifecycle of\\ncurrent and noncurrent versions of objects.\\n\\nThere are per-request transition charges to move data into any supported S3 storage\\nclass\\nand charges to store the transitioned objects in the storage class. For more information,\\nsee **Lifecycle Transition requests** pricing on the **Requests\\n& data retrievals** tab and **Storage pricing** on the\\n**Storage** tab of the Amazon S3\\npricing page\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/help-panel/AmazonS3/latest/console/hp-lifecycle-rule-edit-page.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Lifecycle rule details\",\"context\":\"# Lifecycle rule details\\n\\nYou can configure Amazon S3 Lifecycle rules to store your objects cost-effectively\\nthroughout their lifetime. You can instruct Amazon S3 to transition objects to less-expensive\\nstorage classes or to archive or delete objects.\\n\\nUse this page to see the scope of the selected S3 Lifecycle rule. You can also view\\ntransition and expiration actions for current and noncurrent object versions, based\\non your\\nlifecycle rule.\\n\\nFor **Current version actions**, you can see the following\\ninformation:\\n\\n* Since object creation, *the number of days* after\\n which a current version will be transitioned and *the storage\\n class* to transition that version to.\\n* Since object creation, *the number of days* after\\n which a current version will be expired.\\n\\nFor **Noncurrent versions actions**, you can see the following\\ninformation:\\n\\n* Since an object became noncurrent, *the number of\\n days* after which a noncurrent version will be transitioned and\\n *the storage class* to transition that version\\n to.\\n* After the transition, *the number of newest noncurrent\\n versions* to retain.\\n* Since an object became noncurrent, *the number of\\n days* to permanent deletion and *the number of\\n newest noncurrent versions* to retain afterward.\\n\\nUnder **Delete expired object delete markers or incomplete multipart\\nuploads**, there are two sections of configuration information:\\n\\n* You can see if your lifecycle rule is configured to delete expired object delete\\n markers. Once the data is\\nprocessed, the source and raw data layers are rarely\\naccessed. As a result, transitioning them to infrequent and\\narchive storage class could save money. Apply life cycle\\npolicies to the source, staging, and other data sets that\\nare processed and would no longer be needed.\\n\\nCreate lifecycle policies to clean up incomplete multipart\\nuploads. Also, you can organize data to make life cycle\\npolicies simpler and more effective. For example, keep all\\nsource data under one prefix so you can have a single\\nlifecycle policy for all the source data sets rather than\\none for each source prefix. In addition, use lifecycle\\npolicies to delete many objects to avoid S3 API costs.\\nFinally, if your bucket is versioned, ensure there is a rule\\naction for both current and non-current objects to either\\ntransition or expire\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/cost-modeling-data-lakes/cost-optimization-in-analytics-services.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Check S3 lifecycle cost documentation"}

{"id": "d3677b0b-8b41-4ecf-aff3-2625bab0e152", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "S3 lifecycle rules save money in a few ways. They're listed here from lowest risk to highest.

## 1. Clean up waste first
- **Abort incomplete multipart uploads.** Add a rule that aborts them after 7 days or so. Failed uploads keep accruing storage charges and don't show up in a normal object listing.
- **Expire noncurrent versions** on versioned buckets. Set a number of days since the object became noncurrent. You can also keep only the newest N noncurrent versions. Old versions often make up much of the bill on versioned buckets.
- **Remove expired object delete markers.** They're harmless individually, but they pile up and slow down listings.

## 2. Transition data to cheaper storage classes
Move objects as they cool down. A typical ladder looks like this:
- **S3 Standard** for hot data.
- **Standard-IA** or **One Zone-IA** after 30 days or more, for data you read occasionally. One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, so use it only for data you can recreate.
- **Glacier Instant Retrieval** for archive data you still need in milliseconds.
- **Glacier Flexible Retrieval** or **Deep Archive** for data you rarely or never read.

If you can't predict access patterns, **S3 Intelligent-Tiering** moves objects between tiers automatically. A lifecycle rule can move objects into it.

## 3. Expire data you don't need
Add expiration actions for logs, temp files, and processed staging data. Expiration is permanent. For anything important, turn on versioning, Object Lock, MFA delete, or replication first.

## Pitfalls that can raise your bill
- **Small objects.** By default, S3 won't transition objects smaller than 128 KB. Per-object transition request charges and per-object metadata overhead can outweigh the savings on small files. Compress or aggregate small objects before archiving them. Use an object size filter if you need to override the default.
- **Minimum storage durations.** IA and Glacier classes bill for a minimum period, such as 30 days for Standard-IA and 90 days for Glacier classes. Transitioning data that you'll soon delete or overwrite costs you more.
- **Retrieval fees.** Moving frequently read data to IA or archive classes can cost more than leaving it in Standard.
- **Transition request charges.** Each object transitioned incurs a request charge. Millions of tiny objects can make this significant.
- **Versioned buckets.** Add actions for both current and noncurrent versions, or old versions stay in Standard indefinitely.

## How to scope rules
- Use **prefixes, tags, or size filters** so each rule only touches the right data. Keeping data under consistent prefixes, such as `raw/`, `logs/`, and `tmp/`, makes rules much simpler.
- Before you pick transition days, look at **S3 Storage Lens** or **Storage Class Analysis**. They show how much of your data is cold and how old it is.

## A sample rule set for a logs bucket
- Day 30: transition to Standard-IA.
- Day 90: transition to Glacier Instant Retrieval or Flexible Retrieval.
- Day 365: expire.
- Abort incomplete multipart uploads after 7 days.
- Expire noncurrent versions after 30 days.

I can look at your actual buckets if you'd like. I'd check which ones have no lifecycle configuration, which ones have versioning on, and which ones have incomplete multipart uploads. That would show where the biggest savings are. Applying a lifecycle configuration would be a change to your account that needs your approval. Tell me which account to look in and I'll start.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
